quizQuestions.question: IBM interviewers frequently open with this: which four concepts make up the core pillars of Object-Oriented Programming?
options: Compilation, linking, loading, execution
Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction
Normalization, indexing, joins, transactions
Stacks, queues, trees, graphs
quizQuestions.explanation: Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction are the four pillars of OOP, and IBM's technical rounds routinely start here before drilling into specifics.

quizQuestions.question: A common IBM Java-round question: what is the key difference between method overloading and method overriding?
options: Overloading happens at runtime, overriding at compile time
Overloading is resolved at compile time (same class, different signature); overriding is resolved at runtime (subclass redefines a superclass method)
They are the same thing with different names
Overriding requires a static method; overloading requires a final method
quizQuestions.explanation: Overloading is compile-time (static) polymorphism based on differing method signatures in the same class; overriding is runtime (dynamic) polymorphism where a subclass redefines an inherited method.

quizQuestions.question: What does declaring a variable or method `static` in Java mean?
options: It belongs to the class rather than any single instance, shared across all objects
It can never be changed after initialization
It is automatically thread-safe
It is only visible within the same package
quizQuestions.explanation: A static member belongs to the class itself, not to any particular instance, and is shared by all instances of the class.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement about Java constructors is correct?
options: A constructor must have a return type of void
A constructor has the same name as its class and no return type at all
A class can have at most one constructor
Constructors cannot be overloaded
quizQuestions.explanation: A constructor shares its class's name, has no return type (not even void), and a class may define multiple overloaded constructors.

quizQuestions.question: What is the essential requirement for a recursive function to terminate correctly?
options: It must call itself an even number of times
It must have a base case that stops further recursive calls
It must use a while loop internally
It must return void
quizQuestions.explanation: Every correct recursive function needs a base case reached in a finite number of steps, or it recurses indefinitely and overflows the call stack.

quizQuestions.question: In Java, what's the difference between a checked and an unchecked exception?
options: Checked exceptions must be declared or caught at compile time; unchecked (RuntimeException) exceptions are not enforced by the compiler
Checked exceptions only occur in production; unchecked only in tests
Unchecked exceptions can only be thrown from static methods
There is no difference in modern Java
quizQuestions.explanation: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception, excluding RuntimeException) must be declared with `throws` or caught, while unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) are not compiler-enforced.

quizQuestions.topic: Data Structures - Arrays vs Linked Lists
quizQuestions.question: What is the main trade-off between arrays and linked lists?
options: Arrays give O(1) random access but costly insert/delete in the middle; linked lists give O(1) insert/delete at a known node but O(n) access
Linked lists always use less memory than arrays
Arrays cannot store primitive types
Linked lists support random access in O(1) time
quizQuestions.explanation: Arrays offer constant-time indexed access but shifting elements for insertion/deletion is O(n); linked lists offer O(1) insertion/deletion at a known position but only sequential O(n) access.

quizQuestions.question: Which ordering discipline does a Stack follow, as opposed to a Queue?
options: FIFO (First In, First Out)
LIFO (Last In, First Out)
Random access order
Priority order only
quizQuestions.explanation: A stack is LIFO — the last element pushed is the first popped — while a queue is FIFO, serving elements in the order they arrived.

quizQuestions.question: What is the main behavioral difference between a HashMap and a TreeMap in Java?
options: HashMap keeps keys sorted; TreeMap does not
HashMap gives average O(1) get/put with no ordering guarantee; TreeMap gives O(log n) get/put but keeps keys in sorted order
TreeMap cannot store null keys or values under any circumstance
HashMap and TreeMap have identical time complexity for all operations
quizQuestions.explanation: HashMap offers average constant-time operations with no ordering, while TreeMap is backed by a red-black tree, giving logarithmic operations but sorted key iteration.

quizQuestions.question: When would a LinkedList typically outperform an ArrayList in Java?
options: When you need frequent random-index reads
When you frequently insert/remove elements at the beginning or middle of the list
When memory overhead per element must be minimized
LinkedList always outperforms ArrayList
quizQuestions.explanation: LinkedList avoids the O(n) shifting ArrayList needs for mid-list insert/remove, at the cost of O(n) indexed access and higher per-node memory overhead.

quizQuestions.question: What distinguishes a shallow copy from a deep copy of an object?
options: A shallow copy duplicates primitive fields but shares references to nested objects; a deep copy also recursively duplicates the nested objects
A deep copy is always faster than a shallow copy
A shallow copy only works on interfaces
There is no practical difference in Java
quizQuestions.explanation: A shallow copy copies top-level fields, so mutable nested objects are still shared between original and copy; a deep copy recursively clones nested objects too, fully isolating the two.

quizQuestions.question: What does it mean for a piece of code to be 'thread-safe'?
options: It runs faster when multiple threads use it
It behaves correctly when accessed by multiple threads concurrently, without corrupting shared state
It can only be executed by one thread ever
It automatically parallelizes itself across CPU cores
quizQuestions.explanation: Thread-safe code produces correct results and preserves invariants even when multiple threads call into it concurrently, typically via synchronization or immutability.

quizQuestions.question: What is the key difference between multithreading and multiprocessing?
options: Multithreading runs multiple threads sharing one process's memory space; multiprocessing runs multiple independent processes each with its own memory space
Multiprocessing is only possible on a single CPU core
They are interchangeable terms for the same mechanism
Multithreading always requires a distributed system
quizQuestions.explanation: Threads within a process share memory (fast communication, but risk of race conditions), while separate processes are isolated with their own memory space (safer, but costlier inter-process communication).

quizQuestions.question: In Java's concurrency API, what is the main difference between Runnable and Callable?
options: Runnable can return a result and throw checked exceptions; Callable cannot
Callable can return a result (via `call()`) and throw checked exceptions; Runnable's `run()` returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions
Runnable is only usable with virtual threads
There is no meaningful difference
quizQuestions.explanation: Callable<V>.call() can return a value and declare checked exceptions, while Runnable.run() returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions.

quizQuestions.question: What guarantee does Java's `volatile` keyword provide?
options: It makes compound operations like increment atomic
It ensures a variable's writes are immediately visible to all threads, preventing thread-local caching of a stale value
It prevents a variable from ever being garbage collected
It automatically synchronizes every method in the class
quizQuestions.explanation: volatile guarantees visibility — every read sees the latest write from any thread — but it does not make compound actions like `count++` atomic.

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary purpose of Java's garbage collector?
options: To compile Java bytecode into native machine code
To automatically reclaim memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference
To optimize SQL queries at runtime
To manage thread scheduling
quizQuestions.explanation: The garbage collector automatically identifies and frees memory used by objects no longer reachable by the running program, removing the need for manual memory management.

quizQuestions.question: Why is Java's `String` class immutable?
options: Immutability makes strings automatically faster to concatenate
It enables safe sharing across threads, safe use as a HashMap key (stable hashCode), and string-pool reuse, without another piece of code ever changing the value unexpectedly
Immutable classes cannot implement interfaces
Java requires all final classes to be immutable
quizQuestions.explanation: String immutability enables safe sharing between threads and callers, a stable hashCode for use as a map key, and safe reuse of interned string-pool literals.

quizQuestions.topic: Java - final vs finally vs finalize
quizQuestions.question: What do `final`, `finally`, and `finalize` each do in Java?
options: They are three names for the same keyword in different Java versions
`final` prevents reassignment/overriding/subclassing; `finally` is a block that always executes after try/catch; `finalize` was a (now-deprecated) hook called before garbage collection
All three control access modifiers
`finalize` is a loop construct and `finally` is a variable modifier
quizQuestions.explanation: `final` marks something as non-modifiable/non-overridable, `finally` is a try-block clause guaranteed to run, and `finalize()` was a deprecated Object method once used for pre-GC cleanup.

quizQuestions.question: What problem does the Singleton design pattern solve, and what's a key concern when applying it in multithreaded code?
options: It ensures a class has exactly one instance and provides a global access point; naive lazy initialization must be made thread-safe to avoid creating two instances under concurrent first access
It guarantees a class can never be subclassed
It automatically load-balances requests across instances
It has no relevance to multithreading
quizQuestions.explanation: Singleton restricts a class to one instance with a global access point; a naive lazy-init implementation is a classic race condition unless guarded (double-checked locking, enum singleton, or eager init).

quizQuestions.question: What does the Observer design pattern let you do?
options: Restrict a class to a single instance
Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object (the subject) changes state, all its registered dependents (observers) are notified automatically
Convert an incompatible interface into one a client expects
Serialize an object graph to disk
quizQuestions.explanation: Observer defines a publish/subscribe relationship: when the subject's state changes, every registered observer is notified — the pattern behind event listeners and pub/sub systems.

quizQuestions.question: In a microservices architecture, what problem does the Saga pattern address?
options: Load balancing HTTP traffic across service instances
Managing a distributed transaction across multiple services by breaking it into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails
Encrypting data at rest across services
Caching read-heavy endpoints
quizQuestions.explanation: Since a single ACID transaction can't span multiple services' databases, the Saga pattern chains local transactions with compensating actions, rolling back completed steps if a later step fails.

quizQuestions.question: What is the main trade-off introduced by adding a database index?
options: Indexes only ever help and have no cost
Indexes speed up reads that use the indexed column(s) but add storage overhead and slow down writes, since the index must be updated too
Indexes remove the need for primary keys
Indexes make schema changes impossible
quizQuestions.explanation: An index speeds up lookups/sorts on the indexed column(s) but costs extra storage and slows inserts/updates/deletes because the index structure must be maintained alongside the table.

quizQuestions.question: What do the four ACID properties of a database transaction stand for?
options: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Availability, Concurrency, Integrity, Durability
Atomicity, Caching, Indexing, Delivery
Authentication, Consistency, Idempotency, Durability
quizQuestions.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), and Durability (committed changes survive failures).

quizQuestions.question: What is a defining characteristic that distinguishes a microservices architecture from a monolith?
options: Microservices always use less total infrastructure than a monolith
Microservices split an application into independently deployable services, each typically owning its own data store, communicating over a network (e.g. HTTP/messaging) instead of in-process calls
A monolith cannot use a relational database
Microservices require the frontend and backend to share one process
quizQuestions.explanation: Microservices decompose an application into independently deployable, often independently-data-owning services that communicate over the network, trading operational complexity for independent scaling and deployment.

quizQuestions.question: How does REST typically differ from SOAP as an API style?
options: REST is a strict protocol with a mandatory XML envelope; SOAP is an architectural style with no fixed message format
REST is an architectural style typically using HTTP verbs and JSON, generally lighter-weight; SOAP is a protocol with a strict XML envelope, built-in error handling, and formal contracts (WSDL)
SOAP cannot be used over HTTP
REST requires a SOAP envelope internally
quizQuestions.explanation: REST is an architectural style leaning on HTTP semantics and commonly JSON payloads; SOAP is a stricter, XML-based protocol with a formal envelope/contract (WSDL) and built-in extensions like WS-Security.

quizQuestions.topic: Programming Fundamentals - Compile-time vs Runtime Errors
quizQuestions.question: What is the difference between a compile-time error and a runtime error?
options: A compile-time error is caught by the compiler before the program runs; a runtime error occurs while the program is executing
Runtime errors are always fatal; compile-time errors never are
Compile-time errors only happen in interpreted languages
They are the same category of error in Java
quizQuestions.explanation: Compile-time errors (syntax errors, type mismatches) are caught before execution; runtime errors (like a NullPointerException) only surface while the program is running.

quizQuestions.question: What is a deadlock in the context of concurrent programming?
options: A performance optimization technique
A state where two or more threads/processes are each waiting on a resource held by the other, so none can proceed
A guaranteed outcome of using multiple threads
An error that only happens in single-threaded programs
quizQuestions.explanation: A deadlock occurs when a cycle of threads/processes each hold a resource the next one in the cycle needs, so all of them block forever.

quizQuestions.question: An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache with O(1) get and put is classically implemented using which combination of data structures?
options: A sorted array and binary search
A hash map (for O(1) key lookup) combined with a doubly linked list (for O(1) reordering/eviction of the least recently used entry)
Two separate unsorted arrays
A single min-heap keyed by access time
quizQuestions.explanation: A HashMap gives O(1) key-to-node lookup, and a doubly linked list lets you move a node to the front on access and evict the tail (least recently used) in O(1), avoiding any array shifting.

quizQuestions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a process and a thread?
options: A process is a lightweight unit inside a thread
A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space; a thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process, sharing that process's memory with other threads
Threads always run on separate CPUs from their parent process
There is no practical difference in modern operating systems
quizQuestions.explanation: A process owns its own isolated memory/resources; threads are execution units within a process that share that process's memory space, making them cheaper to create and communicate between.

quizQuestions.question: How does a semaphore differ from a mutex?
options: They are identical synchronization primitives with different names
A mutex allows only one thread to hold the lock at a time (with ownership); a semaphore maintains a count and can allow a fixed number of concurrent holders, without a strict ownership requirement
A semaphore can only be used in single-threaded programs
A mutex can be signaled by a thread that doesn't hold it, but a semaphore cannot
quizQuestions.explanation: A mutex is a binary lock owned by whichever single thread holds it; a semaphore holds a count permitting up to N concurrent accesses and isn't tied to a specific owning thread.

quizQuestions.question: What problem does virtual memory solve for an operating system?
options: It lets programs use more logical memory than is physically installed, by mapping virtual addresses to physical RAM or disk (swap/page file), and isolates each process's address space
It permanently increases the physical RAM in the machine
It replaces the need for a CPU cache
It is only used by database systems, not general programs
quizQuestions.explanation: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, maps pages to physical RAM or disk on demand, and lets total logical memory exceed physical RAM, at the cost of possible page faults.

quizQuestions.topic: Algorithms - Quick Sort vs Merge Sort
quizQuestions.question: What is a key practical trade-off between Quick Sort and Merge Sort?
options: Quick Sort is in-place with good average-case performance but O(n^2) worst case on bad pivots; Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) but typically needs O(n) extra space
Merge Sort cannot sort linked lists
Quick Sort is always stable; Merge Sort never is
They have identical time and space complexity in all cases
quizQuestions.explanation: Quick Sort is typically faster in practice and sorts in-place but degrades to O(n^2) with poor pivot choices; Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases but usually requires linear auxiliary space.

quizQuestions.question: How is the height of a binary tree typically defined and computed?
options: The total number of nodes in the tree
The number of edges (or nodes, by some conventions) on the longest path from the root to a leaf, usually computed recursively as 1 + max(height(left), height(right))
The number of leaf nodes only
It is always equal to log2(number of nodes) for any binary tree
quizQuestions.explanation: Height is the longest root-to-leaf path, computed recursively; it only equals log2(n) for a balanced tree, not for an arbitrary (e.g. skewed) binary tree.

quizQuestions.question: What is the difference between SDLC and STLC?
options: SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) covers the full build process from requirements to deployment; STLC (Software Testing Life Cycle) is the subset of phases focused specifically on planning and executing testing
STLC replaces SDLC entirely in Agile teams
SDLC only applies to waterfall projects
They describe the same set of phases
quizQuestions.explanation: SDLC spans the whole software lifecycle (requirements, design, build, test, deploy, maintain); STLC is the testing-focused subset (test planning, case design, execution, closure) that runs within it.

quizQuestions.question: What is the difference between a local and a global variable?
options: A local variable is accessible only within the block/function/method where it's declared; a global variable is accessible from anywhere in the program (or module/class, depending on the language)
Global variables are always faster to access than local ones
Local variables persist for the entire program's lifetime
There is no difference in compiled languages
quizQuestions.explanation: A local variable's scope is limited to the block or function it's declared in and is typically deallocated when that block exits, while a global variable is visible more broadly and persists for the program's duration.

quizQuestions.question: What does 'marshalling' mean in the context of distributed systems?
options: Load-balancing requests across servers
Converting an object or data structure into a format (e.g. bytes, JSON, XML) that can be transmitted over a network or stored, and reconstructed later (unmarshalling)
Sorting a list before returning it from an API
Encrypting a password before storing it
quizQuestions.explanation: Marshalling serializes in-memory data into a transmittable/storable format for a remote call or persistence; the receiving side unmarshals it back into an in-memory representation.

quizQuestions.question: In a payments/transfers API like this workspace's internal-transfer-service, why does an idempotency key matter?
options: It speeds up the database query for the transfer
It lets a client safely retry a request (e.g. after a timeout) without risking the transfer — and the money movement it represents — being executed twice
It is required only for GET requests
It replaces the need for authentication
quizQuestions.explanation: A client-supplied idempotency key lets the server recognize a retried request as a duplicate of one already processed and return the original result, instead of creating a second journal entry for the same intended transfer.

quizQuestions.question: What is the core invariant enforced by double-entry bookkeeping, as implemented in this workspace's general-ledger-service?
options: Every account must have a positive balance at all times
Every journal entry's total debits must equal its total credits, so money is only ever moved between accounts, never created or destroyed
Every transaction must involve exactly one account
Every transaction must be reversible within 24 hours
quizQuestions.explanation: Double-entry bookkeeping requires every entry's debits to equal its credits; this workspace enforces it structurally in the JournalEntry constructor, so an unbalanced entry can't even be built.

quizQuestions.question: Why does this workspace give each microservice (customer, account, ledger, transfers) its own database rather than one shared database?
options: Shared databases are always slower
It keeps each service's data model private, so services can be deployed, scaled, or changed independently — other services only access it through its HTTP API, never its tables directly
It is required by PostgreSQL
It removes the need for any inter-service communication
quizQuestions.explanation: Database-per-service enforces that a service's internal schema stays private and changeable, since every cross-service interaction goes through its API — a shared database would couple services at the data layer.

quizQuestions.question: What does a circuit breaker pattern do when wrapped around a call like internal-transfer-service calling account-service?
options: It permanently blocks all future calls to that service after any single failure

It tracks recent failures and, once a threshold is crossed, 'opens' to fail fast without calling the downstream service, giving it time to recover before periodically allowing a test call through again
It automatically retries every failed call an unlimited number of times
It encrypts the request payload
quizQuestions.explanation: A circuit breaker trips open after repeated failures, short-circuiting further calls (failing fast) instead of piling up slow/failing requests against a struggling downstream service, then probes periodically to see if it has recovered.
